question: How is the opening hamza of wa-anna read?

positions.position: The canonical readers open the hamza: wa-anna.
positions.reasons: Ibn Mujāhid and al-Fārisī detail the differing fatḥ and kasr patterns in other clauses of the sūra; Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports consensus here, as do al-Qurṭubī, Ibn al-Jazarī, Elmalılı, and Ibn ʿĀshūr. Fatḥ makes this clause part of revelation; al-Farrāʾ notes one pattern that keeps this phrase accusative even while kasr is used elsewhere. Al-Naḥḥās gives the deleted causal lām or coordination as explanations. After quoted speech or a conditional fāʾ, kasr is used, according to Ibn Khālawayh, Abū Ḥātim, al-Qurṭubī, and Sībawayh as reported by al-Ṭabrisī.

positions.position: Ibn Hurmuz and Ṭalḥa read wa-inna with kasra.
positions.reasons: Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn identify these two readers; al-Ālūsī treats it as a fresh sentence, while al-Samīn also allows a causal construal. Sībawayh says it is good Arabic, as reported by al-Fārisī and al-Ṭabrisī; his analogies include Q 23:52 and a line of al-Farazdaq.

turns_on: Whether the clause is read as a dependent fatḥa clause or an independent kasra clause.

question: How does wa-anna al-masājida connect syntactically to its context?

positions.position: It is part of what was revealed to the Prophet, coordinated with the earlier revelation clause.
positions.reasons: Exegetes in Sībawayh's report compare 72:19; al-Fārisī, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Rāzī, Abū Ḥātim, and Ibn ʿĀshūr connect it to 72:1. Al-Naḥḥās also permits a nominative coordinated analysis. Al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī treat it as another revealed item. Al-Nasafī also sees the lām as linking to the following command; Elmalılı connects the passage to 72:16. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the ownership statement explains the command.

positions.position: An unspoken causal lām gives 'because the mosques belong to God, invoke no one with Him.'
positions.reasons: Al-Khalīl's analysis is preferred by Sībawayh, who cites fronting and postponement with lām, analogous preposition deletion, Q 23:52 and 106:1, and labbayka inna l-ḥamda. Al-Fārisī adds 21:92 and 106:1; al-Wāḥidī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Ṭabrisī, and al-Ālūsī draw the same parallels. Al-Zajjāj allows accusative after omitted lām or genitive by Arab usage, citing wa-baladin laysa bihi anīs; al-Naḥḥās gives the accusative. Al-Bayḍāwī objects that the implied lām removes the explanatory work of the fāʾ.

positions.position: With kasra, it can begin a fresh independent sentence.
positions.reasons: Sībawayh regards this as sound Arabic, illustrating independent inna with Q 23:52 and al-Farazdaq's verse; al-Fārisī and al-Ṭabrisī report his judgment. Ibn Hurmuz and Ṭalḥa read accordingly.

turns_on: Whether an omitted causal preposition governs the clause, revelation governs it, or kasra starts a new sentence.

question: What does al-masājid denote?

positions.position: Purpose-built houses of prayer and remembrance, including houses of worship across religious communities.
positions.reasons: Muqātil explicitly includes churches and synagogues alongside Muslim mosques. Ibn ʿAbbās, most commentators cited by al-Wāḥidī and al-Rāzī, al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bursawī, and Elmalılı support worship houses; al-Qurṭubī and Elmalılı prefer the general explanation. Al-Ṭabrisī and Study Quran also give all communities. Elmalılı distinguishes lexical coverage of all faiths from conventional Muslim usage and notes that Muslim-specific mosques had not yet been built. The people of the Book's associationism is cited by Muqātil, Qatāda, Mujāhid, and others. Al-Māwardī calls any prayer place a masjid; al-Farrāʾ, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī, and others give kasra on the singular's jīm for places, while al-Farrāʾ also allows fatḥa; al-Wāḥidī lists exceptional kasra place nouns. Study Quran notes the English 'mosque' derives from masjid.

positions.position: Every place of prostration on earth, whether designated as a mosque or not.
positions.reasons: Al-Ḥasan cites the Prophetic saying that the whole earth was made a mosque for this community; Ibn ʿAṭiyya stresses undesignated places and al-Wāḥidī that earth is its Creator's. Al-Qurṭubī calls the earth-as-mosque report sound. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī objects that permission to worship anywhere does not make every place ordinarily a mosque.

positions.position: The seven bodily parts used in prostration.
positions.reasons: Reports vary in listing face or forehead and nose, hands or palms, knees, feet or toes; their shared seven-part account is retained. They are God's creatures and should bow to no other, say Ibn ʿAṭāʾ, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Ibn al-Anbārī, and others. Ibn al-Anbārī prefers it. Some sources give the singular masjad with fatḥa on jīm, as a bodily prostration point or instrument. The Imam al-Jawād gives this answer when questioned by al-Muʿtaṣim. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says their belonging to God is by religious designation; duʿāʾ there is prostration or prayer.

positions.position: Prostration or the prayers themselves, as a verbal noun.
positions.reasons: Ibn Qutayba compares masjid to maḍrab beside ḍarb, and others give the plural as kinds of prostration or prayer. Al-Ḥasan, Ibn Shajara, and later reports say all prayer belongs to God. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī dismisses this interpretation as unsupported.

positions.position: The Sacred Mosque, Kaʿba, or Mecca, the qibla of other mosques.
positions.reasons: Some explain the plural by its sides, its many mosques, or the many mosques that face it. Ibn ʿAbbās through ʿAṭāʾ names Mecca; Islahi sees a warning to Quraysh and cites 9:17; Kur'an Yolu reports Ibn ʿĀshūr's warning against idols in the Kaʿba. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī objects that a plural does not fit a single place and rejects a sanctuary reading as unsupported.

positions.position: The Sacred Mosque together with Jerusalem.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports this two-place identification among alternatives, but argues that a plural does not fit two places.

turns_on: The scope of masājid and whether its plural denotes buildings, all earth, bodily organs, acts of prostration, or a particular sanctuary.

question: What does saying the mosques are God's signify?

positions.position: They belong to God and are dedicated to His worship, so no partner may be invoked there.
positions.reasons: Al-Kashshāf, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, al-Biqāʿī and others infer exclusive invocation. Al-Biqāʿī extends the point to earth, sky, bodily parts, and senses God created. Al-Ālūsī says association is especially abhorrent in mosques, though unity is due everywhere. The Bursawī ranks the sanctity of the Sacred Mosque, Prophet's Mosque, Jerusalem, congregational, neighborhood, street, and home mosques.

positions.position: Attribution to God honors and distinguishes mosques; human and place names can still identify them.
positions.reasons: Al-Qurṭubī says names may indicate location or endowment, citing a sound horse-racing report involving named sites; al-Bursawī adds builder or location. Al-Qurṭubī says the Sacred House is singled out.

turns_on: Whether the genitive emphasizes exclusive devotion, honor, or both.

question: What does the ban on invoking anyone with God require?

positions.position: Worship, pray to, and invoke God alone, without partners.
positions.reasons: Al-Zajjāj specifies prayer; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 40:60 for duʿāʾ as worship. Qatāda, Mujāhid, Ibn Jurayj and others invoke Jewish and Christian worship in their houses as a warning; al-Māwardī also reports the Meccan Hums talbiya assigning God a partner, and al-Qurṭubī rebukes polytheists in the Sacred Mosque. Al-Bursawī says worshipping another exclusively is worse still. Islahi says alleged deities cannot rescue Quraysh. Al-Naḥḥās says the plural jussive prohibition drops its nūn.

positions.position: The prostrating limbs must not be lowered in prostration to anyone besides their Creator.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAṭāʾ and others connect the ban to the bodily reading of masājid; Ibn al-Anbārī reasons that using God-created limbs for another denies His favor. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reads duʿāʾ as prostration, or prayer containing it.

positions.position: No one has a right to bar God's servants from remembering or invoking Him in His house.
positions.reasons: Sahl's reading is preserved by al-Tustarī and al-Sulamī: what belongs to God cannot be restrained by another.

turns_on: Whether duʿāʾ names worship generally, bodily prostration specifically, or access to invocation.

question: What work does the fāʾ before the prohibition do?

positions.position: It marks the consequence of God's ownership: therefore invoke no one else.
positions.reasons: Al-Bursawī calls it causal. Al-Ālūsī reports that with an implied causal lām some call the fāʾ formally extra, while others hear an implied condition or say the fāʾ reinforces or signals the lām. Al-Bayḍāwī argues that a supplied lām would erase the fāʾ's explanatory value.

question: What event or audience prompted the verse?

positions.position: Distant jinn asked how they could reach the Prophet's mosque and pray with him; the verse assured them worship is accepted where they are.
positions.reasons: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr's report recurs through al-Ṭabarī, al-Jishumī, al-Baghawī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Suyūṭī, and al-Ālūsī. Al-Qurṭubī says the mosque is for remembrance and obedience; Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī state the reassurance about distance.

positions.position: The jinn sought to join prayer in the Prophet's mosque; they were told to pray without mixing with people.
positions.reasons: Al-Aʿmash's version is reported by Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Māwardī, Ibn Kathīr and al-Suyūṭī. Ibn ʿAbbās is cited by al-Suyūṭī for a request for permission to attend.

positions.position: After Quraysh took control of the Kaʿba, the verse assured the Prophet he could worship God anywhere.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān report this occasion and the answer that every place belongs to God.

positions.position: The Meccan Hums' talbiya assigned God a partner, so the verse forbade association.
positions.reasons: Al-Māwardī transmits the report from Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī.

positions.position: It was revealed to Muhammad after the account of the jinn.
positions.reasons: Al-Farrāʾ reports this from Ibn ʿAbbās.

turns_on: The reports name differing immediate settings: distant jinn, separation from people, Quraysh's control of the Kaʿba, or a pagan talbiya.

question: Which mosques existed when the verse was revealed?

positions.position: The Sacred Mosque and the Jerusalem mosque were then the only two.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās's report names Jerusalem as Bayt al-Maqdis or Aelia/Ilyāʾ across Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Kathīr, al-Suyūṭī and al-Ālūsī.

question: What should a person say or do when entering and leaving a mosque?

positions.position: On entering, declare God's oneness and greet the Messenger.
positions.reasons: Al-Thaʿlabī says Muslims adopted this after revelation; al-Ḥasan calls a declaration of sole divinity and invocation Sunnah, since the prohibition implies God's remembrance.

positions.position: Enter right-foot first asking deliverance from the Fire; leave left-foot first asking abundant good and ease.
positions.reasons: Al-Māwardī reports this through al-Ḍaḥḥāk from Ibn ʿAbbās; al-Qurṭubī repeats it and states no grading.

turns_on: The reports give distinct entry remembrance and foot-first supplications.

question: Which activities belong in mosques?

positions.position: Mosques are reserved for worship, supplication, learning, and other acts done for God; ordinary worldly use is improper.
positions.reasons: Al-Thaʿlabī and al-Qurṭubī mention trade, meetings, passageways and mockery; Ibn ʿAṭiyya adds quarrels, oaths and litigation abuse, explaining why he stopped hearing cases in Almeria's congregational mosque. Al-Jishumī says worldly work is disliked. A Prophetic report rejects announcing lost property, because mosques were not built for that.

positions.position: Several practical uses are permitted.
positions.reasons: Al-Qurṭubī permits distributing funds and charity, detention, restraining captives, sleeping, housing the sick, access for neighbors, and truthful poetry.

positions.position: Abū Ḥanīfa permits judicial work in mosques as religious business.
positions.reasons: Al-Jishumī records the juristic disagreement.

positions.position: Al-Shāfiʿī dislikes judicial work in mosques.
positions.reasons: Al-Jishumī records this position; Ibn ʿAṭiyya's Almeria experience illustrates the disturbance litigation can cause.

turns_on: Whether a use serves worship or violates a mosque's dignity, especially judicial disputes.

question: May mosques and comparable public works be endowed?

positions.position: The community agrees that mosques, bridges and cemeteries can be endowed; other property is disputed.
positions.reasons: Al-Qurṭubī states the consensus and identifies the remaining juristic dispute.

question: What do the reports specify about the limbs used in prostration?

positions.position: The Prophet was commanded to prostrate on seven bodily parts.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās lists forehead, hands, knees and toes, sometimes including the nose by gesture; al-ʿAbbās says seven joints prostrate with the servant. Elmalılı and al-Kashshāf repeat the forehead or face, nose, hands, knees and feet variants. The report also forbids gathering hair or clothing during prostration.

positions.position: Eight bones may touch the ground, but seven are obligatory; placing the nose is Sunnah.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṣādiq specifies forehead, palms, knees and big toes as the obligatory seven under the verse.

turns_on: Whether the nose is counted with the forehead among the seven obligatory points or named as an additional recommended point.

question: What does this verse imply for the thief's hand?

positions.position: Cut at the finger joints and leave the palm, because the palm is one of God's prostration points.
positions.reasons: Abū Jaʿfar gave this answer when al-Muʿtaṣim asked where the hand should be cut.

question: What travel and prayer merits are reported for particular mosques?

positions.position: Travel for worship is specified for three mosques.
positions.reasons: Al-Qurṭubī cites the Prophetic report and says hadith authorities transmitted it.

positions.position: Prayer in the Prophet's mosque exceeds a thousand prayers elsewhere, except in the Sacred Mosque.
positions.reasons: Al-Qurṭubī transmits the Prophetic report.

positions.position: Prayer in the Sacred Mosque exceeds a hundred prayers in the Prophet's mosque.
positions.reasons: Ibn al-ʿArabī reports a sound route; al-Qurṭubī affirms reliable transmitters and says he discussed it in his treatment of Ibrāhīm.

turns_on: The reports address separate travel and prayer-reward measures.

question: Is the earth's use as mosque and purifier distinctive to this community?

positions.position: Prayer across the whole earth is a distinctive privilege of Muhammad's community.
positions.reasons: Al-Ālūsī reports the common claim that prior communities were restricted to synagogues and churches, citing a sound hadith about the earth as mosque and purifier.

positions.position: The distinct privilege is the combined gift of the earth as mosque and purifier, especially dry ablution.
positions.reasons: Al-Ālūsī reports this answer to the objection that traveling prophets must have prayed outside worship buildings.

positions.position: The comparison concerns earlier communities, not their prophets.
positions.reasons: Al-Ālūsī offers this answer; he says al-Khiḍr, if alive, belongs to Muhammad's community, citing the statement that Moses would have to follow Muhammad if alive.

turns_on: How to understand the earlier prophets' ability to pray while traveling, and whether the privilege is place, purification, or community scope.

question: How does the verse connect to other verses and the sūra?

positions.position: It follows the jinn's listening and states revealed guidance about God's sole right to worship.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿĀshūr and Kur'an Yolu link it to 72:1; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the jinn story leads into the Prophet's mission, unity, resurrection and protection from error. Elmalılı says the clauses explain rushd, the right path, and links this verse with 72:16.

positions.position: Other verses reinforce the consecration and proper use of God's houses.
positions.reasons: Al-Kashshāf cites 2:114 against blocking God's name; al-Qurṭubī cites 22:26 on purifying His House; Elmalılı compares 2:114 and Islahi cites 9:17 for the general rule alongside the Sacred House.

turns_on: Which nearby narrative or other Qur'anic passage supplies the explanatory link.

question: What inward meaning is given to mosques and invocation?

positions.position: Mosques signify the perfection of each faculty in submission to the heart, and of heart and spirit, where God's right or attribute appears.
positions.reasons: Al-Qāshānī extends 'mosques' to the perfection of anything.

positions.position: Invoking another means following the ego's aims, caprice, pleasures and desires.
positions.reasons: Al-Qāshānī calls these associations with God according to one's nature.

positions.position: The heart's mosques should be purified for God's Greatest Name alone.
positions.reasons: Al-Bursawī excludes partial names from the heart's sanctuary.

positions.position: Bodily prostration purifies limbs used to pursue sins and desires.
positions.reasons: Al-Bursawī says prostration atones and erases sin through the very limbs that carry out action.

turns_on: The inward readers apply the mosque and the command to faculties, desires, the heart, or bodily purification.

question: What pausal vowel rules are discussed alongside this passage?

positions.position: Reciters bar rawm on a non-nunated fatḥa, while grammarians permit it across all three vowels.
positions.reasons: Ibn al-Jazarī says reciters count rawm as part of the vowel whereas grammarians regard it as hidden movement, exemplified by an yaḍriba; Sībawayh allows rawm with accusative or genitive but not ishmām, supporting the grammarians.

positions.position: Rawm differs from ikhtilās and ikhfaʾ in the reciters' usage.
positions.reasons: Ibn al-Jazarī equates the latter two, notes loose use of ikhfaʾ for rawm, and questions al-Dānī's equation.

positions.position: A feminine tāʾ changed to hāʾ at pause allows neither rawm nor ishmām; retained written tāʾ allows both.
positions.reasons: Ibn al-Jazarī explains that the retained consonant normally bears the vowel.

positions.position: At pause, an open doubled final consonant keeps its shadda and takes sukūn.
positions.reasons: Ibn al-Jazarī allows two consecutive quiescent letters at pause and rejects stopping on fatḥa.

turns_on: Different accounts of rawm and different consonant shapes at pause.
